title: Two Sum
description:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: Because nums[0] + nums[1] == 9, we return [0,1].

hints: A brute force approach checks every pair of numbers, resulting in O(n²) time complexity.
Can we store previously seen numbers and quickly check if the complement exists?
A HashMap allows O(1) lookup for the complement.
intuition: Instead of searching the entire array for the complement of every number, store previously seen numbers in a HashMap. This converts repeated searches into constant-time lookups, reducing the overall complexity from O(n²) to O(n).

patternExplanation.name: Complement Lookup using HashMap
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Store visited elements and check whether the required complement already exists.

bruteForce.reason: Every element is compared against every other element.

optimal.reason: Each element is processed once and HashMap lookup takes O(1).

approaches.name: Brute Force
HashMap

edgeCases.reason: Duplicate numbers can form the answer.
HashMap solution works regardless of sign.
Array length can be as small as 2.

pitfalls: Using the same element twice.
Adding the current element to the HashMap before checking its complement.
Assuming the array is sorted.
Forgetting that indices, not values, must be returned.
followUpQuestions: What if the array is sorted?
Can you solve it with O(1) extra space?
How would you return all valid pairs?
How would you solve this problem for a stream of incoming numbers?
What changes if multiple solutions are allowed?

notes.title: HashMap Pattern
notes.description: Store elements seen so far and check whether the complement exists in O(1) time.

notes.title: Why O(n) Works
notes.description: Each element is visited exactly once and each HashMap operation is O(1) on average.

notes.title: Common Mistake
notes.description: Insert into the HashMap after checking for the complement to avoid matching the same element.

timeComplexity: O(n) - We only need to traverse both strings once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) - Since the size of the character set is fixed (26 lowercase letters), the extra space is constant.

title: Contains Duplicate
description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.

examples.explanation: The element 1 appears twice.
All elements are unique.

hints: A brute force solution compares every element with every other element.
Can we remember numbers we've already seen?
A HashSet provides O(1) average lookup time.
intuition: The moment we encounter a number that has already been seen before, we know a duplicate exists. Instead of repeatedly searching the array, we can store visited numbers inside a HashSet and check membership in constant time.

patternExplanation.name: Seen Elements Tracking
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Store elements as you traverse and check whether the current element already exists.

bruteForce.reason: Every element is compared against every other element.

optimal.reason: Each element is processed once and HashSet lookup is O(1).

approaches.name: Brute Force
HashSet

edgeCases.reason: Single element arrays cannot contain duplicates.
HashSet works regardless of value sign.

pitfalls: Using nested loops for large inputs.
Confusing duplicate values with duplicate indices.
Forgetting that only existence of duplicates matters.
followUpQuestions: How would you return the duplicate values instead of true/false?
How would you count occurrences of each element?
Can you solve it without extra space?
What changes if the array is sorted?
How would you handle a stream of incoming numbers?

notes.title: HashSet Pattern
notes.description: Whenever duplicate detection is required, HashSet is often the first optimal solution.

notes.title: Early Exit Optimization
notes.description: Return immediately once a duplicate is found.

notes.title: Interview Tip
notes.description: Mention sorting as an alternative solution with O(n log n) time and O(1) space.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description:
Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i].

The solution must run in O(n) time and you cannot use the division operator.

examples.explanation: For each index, multiply all elements except itself.
Since there is one zero, only the index containing zero gets a non-zero product.

constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Brute force would compute the product for every index separately.
Notice that answer[i] = product of left elements × product of right elements.
Can we precompute prefix and suffix products?
Can we optimize space further?
intuition: Instead of calculating the product for every index independently, we can precompute the product of all elements to the left and all elements to the right. The answer for any position becomes leftProduct × rightProduct. This avoids repeated multiplication and achieves O(n) time complexity.

patternExplanation.name: Prefix and Suffix Product
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Precompute information from the left and right side of every index.

bruteForce.reason: For each element, we calculate the product of all other elements.

better.reason: Store prefix and suffix products separately.

optimal.reason: Reuse the output array to store prefix products and calculate suffix products on the fly.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix + Suffix Arrays
Optimal Prefix-Suffix

edgeCases.reason: Multiple zeros make every result zero.
Sign changes depending on the count of negative values.

pitfalls: Using division when the problem explicitly forbids it.
Not handling zero values correctly.
Forgetting that prefix excludes the current element.
Incorrect suffix traversal direction.
followUpQuestions: Can you solve it using division?
What changes if multiple zeros exist?
Can this be solved in a single traversal?
How would you solve it for a stream of numbers?
How would you generalize this for a matrix?

notes.title: Core Interview Pattern
notes.description: This is one of the most important Prefix Product problems and is frequently used to test optimization skills.

notes.title: Space Optimization
notes.description: The output array itself can store prefix products, eliminating the need for an extra prefix array.

notes.title: Why Division is Banned
notes.description: Division fails when zeros are present and doesn't test understanding of prefix/suffix techniques.

title: Maximum Subarray
description:
Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.

A subarray is a contiguous non-empty sequence of elements within an array.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum = 6.
The only element itself forms the maximum subarray.
The entire array forms the maximum subarray.

hints: Brute force would generate all possible subarrays and calculate their sums.
For every position, decide whether to extend the current subarray or start a new one.
Keep track of the best sum seen so far while iterating.
intuition: When traversing the array, a negative running sum hurts future subarrays. If the current sum becomes worse than starting fresh from the current element, we reset and begin a new subarray. This greedy observation leads to Kadane's Algorithm.

patternExplanation.name: Kadane's Algorithm
patternExplanation.coreIdea: At every index, choose the maximum between starting a new subarray or extending the existing one.

bruteForce.reason: Generate every subarray and compute its sum.

better.reason: Maintain running sums while generating subarrays.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Kadane's Algorithm

edgeCases.reason: All elements are negative. Answer is the largest element.
Entire array contributes to the answer.

pitfalls: Resetting the running sum to zero blindly.
Failing to handle arrays containing all negative values.
Using extra arrays when not required.
Confusing subsequence with subarray.
followUpQuestions: Can you return the actual subarray instead of just the sum?
How would you solve Maximum Circular Subarray?
Can this be solved using divide and conquer?
What changes if the array is streamed?
How would you find the minimum subarray sum?

notes.title: Interview Favorite
notes.description: Kadane's Algorithm is one of the most frequently asked array patterns in interviews.

notes.title: Greedy + DP
notes.description: Although often called a greedy algorithm, Kadane's can also be viewed as Dynamic Programming.

notes.title: Core Formula
notes.description: currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i])

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description:
Given an integer array nums, find a contiguous non-empty subarray within the array that has the largest product, and return the product.

The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,3] has the largest product = 6.
The result cannot be 2 because [-2,-1] is not a contiguous subarray.
The entire array produces the maximum product.

constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: This looks similar to Maximum Subarray, but multiplication behaves differently than addition.
A negative number can turn the smallest product into the largest product.
Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each position.
intuition: For sum problems, only the maximum running value matters. For product problems, a negative number can flip signs. A very small negative product can suddenly become the largest positive product after multiplying by another negative number. Therefore, we must track both the current maximum and current minimum products.

patternExplanation.name: Max-Min Tracking
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain both the maximum and minimum product ending at every index because negative numbers can swap their roles.

bruteForce.reason: Generate every possible subarray and compute products.

optimal.reason: Track max and min products in a single traversal.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Kadane Variant

edgeCases.reason: Even number of negatives creates a positive product.

pitfalls: Tracking only the maximum product.
Ignoring the effect of negative numbers.
Not swapping max and min when encountering a negative value.
Forgetting that zero resets the running product.
followUpQuestions: Can you return the actual subarray?
How would you solve this in a circular array?
What changes if floating-point numbers are allowed?
Can this be solved using prefix and suffix products?
How would you find the minimum product subarray?

notes.title: Key Observation
notes.description: A negative number can turn the smallest product into the largest product.

notes.title: Relation to Kadane
notes.description: This is often considered the multiplicative version of Kadane's Algorithm.

notes.title: Why Track Minimum?
notes.description: A large negative product may become the future maximum after multiplication by another negative number.

title: Move Zeroes
description:
Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of the array while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements.

You must do this in-place without making a copy of the array.

examples.explanation: All non-zero elements maintain their original order while zeros are moved to the end.
Single element array.
No zeros exist, so the array remains unchanged.

hints: A simple solution is to create a new array and copy all non-zero elements first.
Can we solve it without using extra space?
Use one pointer to track where the next non-zero element should be placed.
intuition: Whenever we encounter a non-zero element, we should move it to the earliest available position. A pointer keeps track of where the next non-zero value belongs. After placing all non-zero elements, the remaining positions are filled with zeros.

patternExplanation.name: Fast-Slow Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use one pointer to scan the array and another pointer to maintain the position for valid elements.

extraArray.reason: Uses a separate array to store non-zero elements.

optimal.reason: Rearranges elements directly within the original array.

approaches.name: Extra Array
Two Pointers (Optimal)
Swap-Based Two Pointers

pitfalls: Using extra space when the problem requires an in-place solution.
Changing the relative order of non-zero elements.
Incorrectly swapping zeros multiple times.
Forgetting to fill remaining positions with zeros.
followUpQuestions: Can you minimize the number of write operations?
How would you move all negative numbers to the end instead?
Can you solve it using a stable partition algorithm?
How would you move all occurrences of a specific value?
What changes if order does not matter?

notes.title: Core Two Pointer Pattern
notes.description: One pointer scans the array while another pointer tracks the next valid insertion position.

notes.title: Stable Rearrangement
notes.description: The relative order of non-zero elements must remain unchanged.

notes.title: Interview Tip
notes.description: Mention both extra-space and in-place approaches before optimizing.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
description:
Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once.

The relative order of the elements should be kept the same.

Return the number of unique elements k.

The first k elements of nums should contain the unique elements in their original order. The remaining elements beyond k are not important.

examples.explanation: There are 2 unique elements: 1 and 2.
The first 5 positions contain all unique values.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Because the array is sorted, duplicates will always appear next to each other.
Maintain one pointer for the last unique element found.
Whenever a new unique value is found, place it in the next available position.
intuition: Since duplicates are adjacent in a sorted array, we only need to compare the current element with the last unique element. A write pointer tracks where the next unique value should be placed, allowing us to overwrite duplicates in-place.

patternExplanation.name: Read-Write Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use one pointer to read through the array and another pointer to write valid elements.

extraArray.reason: Store unique values in a separate array.

optimal.reason: Use two pointers and modify the original array.

approaches.name: Extra Array
Two Pointers (Optimal)

pitfalls: Using extra space despite the in-place requirement.
Forgetting that the array is already sorted.
Comparing against the wrong pointer.
Returning the modified array instead of k.
followUpQuestions: What if each element can appear at most twice?
How would you solve it if the array was not sorted?
Can you return the unique values as a list?
How would you count duplicates removed?
What changes if order does not matter?

notes.title: Sorted Array Advantage
notes.description: Since duplicates are adjacent, we only need to compare neighboring elements.

notes.title: Read vs Write Pointer
notes.description: The read pointer scans all elements while the write pointer tracks where the next unique value belongs.

notes.title: Foundation Pattern
notes.description: This pattern appears in many array and string compression problems.

title: Majority Element
description:
Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element.

The majority element is the element that appears more than ⌊n / 2⌋ times. You may assume that the majority element always exists in the array.

examples.explanation: 3 appears more than n/2 times.
2 appears 4 times out of 7.

hints: A simple approach is to count frequencies using a HashMap.
Can we reduce space usage to O(1)?
Try canceling out different elements instead of counting them.
intuition: The majority element appears more than half the time, so it will always survive cancellation against all other elements. If we pair different elements and cancel them out, the majority element will remain at the end.

patternExplanation.name: Voting / Cancellation Technique
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Pair different elements and cancel them out. The remaining element is the majority.

optimal.reason: Maintain a single candidate and counter.

approaches.name: HashMap Counting
Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm

pitfalls: Assuming sorting is required.
Not understanding why cancellation works.
Forgetting majority element is guaranteed to exist.
Trying to track all frequencies unnecessarily.
followUpQuestions: What if the majority element is not guaranteed to exist?
How would you find all elements appearing more than n/3 times?
Can this be extended to streaming data?
What if the input is distributed across machines?
Can you solve it using divide and conquer?

notes.title: Key Insight
notes.description: Pairing different elements cancels them out, leaving the majority element.

notes.title: Why It Works
notes.description: Because the majority element appears more than n/2 times, it cannot be fully canceled.

notes.title: Interview Importance
notes.description: This is one of the most frequently asked array problems in top tech companies.

title: Merge Sorted Array
description:
You are given two sorted integer arrays nums1 and nums2, and two integers m and n representing the number of elements in nums1 and nums2 respectively.

Merge nums2 into nums1 as one sorted array.

The final sorted array should not be returned by the function, but instead be stored inside nums1. nums1 has a size of m + n, where the first m elements denote the elements that should be merged, and the last n elements are set to 0 and should be ignored.

examples.explanation: Both arrays are merged in sorted order into nums1.
No elements to merge from nums2.

hints: If we start merging from the beginning, we may overwrite values in nums1.
Instead, try filling nums1 from the end.
Always place the larger element at the last available position.
intuition: Since nums1 has extra space at the end, we can avoid overwriting by filling it backwards. We compare the largest elements of nums1 and nums2 and place the larger one at the end of nums1.

patternExplanation.name: Reverse Two Pointers
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use two pointers starting from the end of both arrays to avoid overwriting data.

bruteForce.reason: Merge both arrays into a new array and sort it.

optimal.reason: Use two pointers from the end and merge in-place.

approaches.name: Extra Array + Sort
Three Pointers (Optimal)

edgeCases.case: All elements in nums2 are smaller/larger

pitfalls: Merging from the front and overwriting nums1.
Forgetting to copy remaining elements from nums2.
Incorrect pointer initialization.
Not handling m = 0 or n = 0 cases.
followUpQuestions: Can you merge without modifying nums1?
What if nums1 does not have extra space?
How would you merge k sorted arrays?
Can this be extended to linked lists?
What if arrays are in descending order?

notes.title: Key Insight
notes.description: Start merging from the end to avoid overwriting elements in nums1.

notes.title: Why Backward Works
notes.description: nums1 has empty space at the end, so we safely fill from right to left.

notes.title: Interview Importance
notes.description: This is a classic test of pointer manipulation and in-place array handling.

title: Find Pivot Index
description:
Given an array of integers nums, calculate the pivot index of this array.

The pivot index is the index where the sum of all the numbers strictly to the left of the index is equal to the sum of all the numbers strictly to the right of the index.

If the index is on the left edge, the left sum is 0. If the index is on the right edge, the right sum is 0.

Return the leftmost pivot index. If no such index exists, return -1.

examples.explanation: Left sum = 1+7+3 = 11, Right sum = 5+6 = 11
No index satisfies left sum equals right sum
Left sum = 0, Right sum = 1 + (-1) = 0

hints: Try computing total sum of the array first.
As you iterate, maintain left sum and derive right sum using totalSum - leftSum - current element.
You don't need nested loops.
intuition: Instead of recomputing left and right sums for every index, we compute the total sum once. Then while iterating, we maintain a running left sum and calculate right sum in constant time using subtraction.

patternExplanation.name: Running Prefix Sum
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain cumulative sum while iterating and use total sum to compute right side efficiently.

bruteForce.reason: For each index, compute left and right sums separately.

optimal.reason: Use total sum and maintain running left sum.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix Sum (Optimal)

edgeCases.reason: Single element always satisfies pivot condition
All indices can be valid pivots but we return the first
Return -1 when no balance point is found

pitfalls: Recomputing sums repeatedly leading to O(n²) solution
Forgetting to subtract current element while computing right sum
Returning last pivot instead of first
Not handling negative numbers correctly
followUpQuestions: What if there are multiple pivot indices?
Can you solve it using prefix array?
What if the array is dynamic and updates frequently?
How would you find pivot for subarray queries?
Can you extend this to 2D matrices?

notes.title: Core Insight
notes.description: Right sum can always be derived instead of recomputed.

notes.title: Optimization Trick
notes.description: totalSum - leftSum - nums[i] gives right sum in O(1).

notes.title: Interview Importance
notes.description: Frequently asked to test prefix sum understanding.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of subarrays whose sum equals k.

A subarray is a contiguous non-empty sequence of elements within an array.

examples.explanation: Subarrays are [1,1] (first two) and [1,1] (last two).
Subarrays are [1,2] and [3].

hints: Brute force checks all subarrays and sums them individually.
Can prefix sum help us avoid recomputing sums repeatedly?
If prefixSum[i] - prefixSum[j] = k, then a valid subarray exists between j and i.
We can store prefix sums in a HashMap to count occurrences.
intuition: Instead of recomputing sums for every subarray, we maintain a running prefix sum. If at any point (currentSum - k) has been seen before, it means a subarray ending at the current index has sum k. We use a HashMap to count how many times each prefix sum has occurred.

patternExplanation.name: Prefix Sum with Frequency Map
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Store frequency of prefix sums and check if (currentSum - k) exists.

bruteForce.reason: Check every subarray and compute sum repeatedly.

optimal.reason: Each prefix sum is processed once and stored in HashMap.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix Sum + HashMap

edgeCases.reason: Zero sum subarrays with negatives included

pitfalls: Not initializing map with {0:1}
Forgetting overlapping subarrays
Assuming array contains only positive numbers
Using sliding window (invalid for negative numbers)
followUpQuestions: What if all numbers are positive?
Can you return actual subarrays instead of count?
How would you solve it for streaming data?
What if we only want longest subarray with sum k?
Can this be extended to 2D matrices?

notes.title: Key Insight
notes.description: If prefixSum[i] - prefixSum[j] = k, then subarray j+1 to i has sum k.

notes.title: Why HashMap Works
notes.description: It stores how many times a prefix sum has occurred, enabling O(1) lookup.

notes.title: Common Mistake
notes.description: Using sliding window incorrectly when negative numbers are present.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description:
Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i].

You must solve it without using division and in O(n) time.

examples.explanation: Each index contains product of all elements except itself.
Zero affects all products except where it is excluded.

hints: Think in terms of prefix products and suffix products.
Each element’s answer is product of everything on left * product of everything on right.
Avoid recomputing products repeatedly.
intuition: Instead of computing full product for every index, we split the problem into two parts: product of all elements to the left and product of all elements to the right. Multiply them to get the final result for each index.

patternExplanation.name: Prefix and Postfix Product Arrays
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Build left products in one pass and right products in another pass, then combine.

bruteForce.reason: Compute product for each index separately.

optimal.reason: Use output array and constant extra space for prefix/postfix.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix + Postfix (Optimal)

edgeCases.reason: Multiple zeros make most outputs zero.

pitfalls: Using division (not allowed in interview variant).
Forgetting to handle zeros properly.
Allocating extra prefix and suffix arrays unnecessarily.
Not updating result in-place style optimization.
followUpQuestions: Can you solve it using constant extra space?
What if division is allowed?
How would you handle streaming input?
Can you return prefix and suffix arrays separately?
What changes if multiplication is modulo-based?

notes.title: Key Insight
notes.description: Every answer is product of left side × right side.

notes.title: Optimization Trick
notes.description: Reuse result array for prefix product to save space.

notes.title: Interview Importance
notes.description: One of the most frequently asked array transformation problems.

title: Longest Subarray with Sum K
description:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum equals k.

If no such subarray exists, return 0.

examples.explanation: The subarray [1,-1,5,-2] has sum 3 and length 4.
The subarray [-1,2] has sum 1 and length 2.

hints: Brute force checks every possible subarray.
Use prefix sums to avoid recalculating sums repeatedly.
If prefixSum - k exists, a valid subarray is found.
Store the FIRST occurrence of every prefix sum.
intuition: Suppose current prefix sum is S. If a previous prefix sum S-k exists, then the elements between them sum to k. To maximize length, we want the earliest occurrence of S-k, so we store only the first occurrence of each prefix sum.

patternExplanation.name: Prefix Sum with Earliest Occurrence
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Store the first index where each prefix sum appears to maximize subarray length.

optimal.reason: Single pass with HashMap storing prefix sums.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix Sum + HashMap

edgeCases.reason: Sliding window fails, prefix sum is needed.

pitfalls: Overwriting earlier prefix sum indices.
Using sliding window with negative numbers.
Not handling prefixSum == k case separately.
Storing latest occurrence instead of first occurrence.
followUpQuestions: Can you return the actual subarray?
What if all numbers are positive?
How would you count all subarrays with sum k?
What if the array is streamed continuously?
Can this be extended to matrices?

notes.title: Store First Occurrence
notes.description: First occurrence gives maximum possible length.

notes.title: Difference from Subarray Sum Equals K
notes.description: That problem counts subarrays, this one maximizes length.

notes.title: Common Interview Trap
notes.description: Many candidates overwrite HashMap entries and lose longer answers.

title: Container With Most Water
description:
You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]).

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container such that the container contains the maximum amount of water.

Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Notice that you may not slant the container.

examples.explanation: The maximum area is formed by height[1] = 8 and height[8] = 7. Width = 7, Height = 7, Area = 49.
Only one container can be formed.

hints: The area is determined by the shorter line and the distance between the lines.
Brute force checks every pair of lines.
Can we eliminate some pairs without checking them?
Move the pointer pointing to the smaller height.
intuition: For any two lines, the water level is limited by the shorter line. If we move the taller line inward, the width decreases and the limiting height doesn't improve. Therefore, the only useful move is to advance the pointer at the shorter line in hopes of finding a taller boundary.

patternExplanation.name: Two Pointers with Greedy Elimination
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Start with the widest container and shrink the window while trying to improve the limiting height.

bruteForce.reason: Check every possible pair of lines.

optimal.reason: Each pointer moves at most n times.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Two Pointers (Optimal)

pitfalls: Moving the taller pointer instead of the shorter one.
Assuming larger heights always produce larger areas.
Ignoring width reduction while moving pointers.
Using brute force for large constraints.
followUpQuestions: Why is moving the shorter pointer always safe?
Can you prove the greedy approach?
What changes if lines can be slanted?
Can this be solved using dynamic programming?
How would you visualize the pointer movement?

notes.title: Key Formula
notes.description: Area = min(height[left], height[right]) × (right - left)

notes.title: Greedy Observation
notes.description: The shorter line limits the area. Moving the taller line cannot increase the limiting height.

notes.title: Interview Importance
notes.description: One of the most frequently asked Two Pointer problems in coding interviews.
